clue.text: Dunderheads tearing up the grisly bills

indicators.note: tearing something up rips it apart, so the words before it are pulled apart and reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone shreds a set of gruesome bills and is called a fool for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tearing up' rearranges THE GRISLY BILLS, all fourteen letters, into the answer. SILLY BLIGHTERS is British slang for foolish fellows.
explanation.definitionFit: A blighter is a mildly abusive British word for a person, so silly ones are dimwits or fools.

clue.text: An insect's cutting lines

indicators.note: the first two letters of insect's, read separately, put the article inside the factions

parts.note: sects are religious factions; the word insect's splits as in plus sect's

explanation.surface: A bug's mandibles described as its slicing edges.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'insect's' into 'in sect's' and 'in' becomes the container signal. Secant comes from the Latin for cutting; in geometry it is a line that cuts a curve.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry a secant is a straight line that crosses a curve at two or more points, cutting through it.

clue.text: What the amphibian can do without being hypocritical

definitions.text: What the amphibian can do without being hypocritical

parts.words: What the amphibian can do without being hypocritical
parts.note: a frog lives both in water and on land, so it has two lives quite innocently, while the phrase usually means living deceitfully

explanation.surface: A question about what a frog can manage while remaining sincere.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means keeping a secret second existence; an amphibian literally has a double life, aquatic and terrestrial, with no deceit involved.
explanation.definitionFit: Amphibians spend part of their existence in water and part on land, a twofold mode of living.

clue.text: A tug from New England

definitions.meaning: a Yankee, originally a New Englander, shortened to the informal form

explanation.definitionFit: A sharp pull is a jerk on a rope, and the informal short form of Yankee describes a person from the north-eastern United States.

clue.text: A willing disposition?

parts.note: read 'willing' as making a will, and a disposition as the handing over of property, rather than an eager temperament

explanation.surface: A phrase praising someone's eager, cooperative temperament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Willing' seems to mean eager; here it means done by will, and 'disposition' is the legal giving away of property.
explanation.definitionFit: A bequest left to someone in a will is a handing-over of property by testament.

clue.text: The most rudimentary of Zola's novels?

definitions.text: The most rudimentary of Zola's novels?

parts.words: The most rudimentary of Zola's novels?
parts.note: an adjective meaning at the earliest embryonic stage is also the title of an Emile Zola novel about miners

explanation.surface: A question about which book by Zola is the most primitive.
explanation.walkthrough: Zola's 1885 novel of a mining strike shares its title with an adjective meaning in the seed or bud stage, hence 'most rudimentary'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes something in an embryonic, budding state, and is also the title of Zola's coal-mining novel.

clue.text: A sporting bunch of racketeers!

parts.note: racketeers are usually gangsters; here they are players who wield rackets, and a sporting bunch is their association

explanation.surface: An ironic remark about a gang of good-natured criminals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racketeers' suggests organised crime; read it as people with rackets, and the bunch becomes a membership organisation for a racket game.
explanation.definitionFit: A local association whose members play a racket sport on courts together.

clue.text: Does it take pride to cause such amusement?

definitions.text: Does it take pride to cause such amusement?

parts.words: Does it take pride to cause such amusement?
parts.note: a pride is a group of lions, whose noise is a roar, so a pride could produce the loud sounds of mirth

explanation.surface: A question whether vanity is needed to make people laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pride' seems to mean self-esteem; it is a group of lions, whose roars fit the phrase for loud hearty laughter.
explanation.definitionFit: Loud bursts of hilarity from an audience are described with a lion's noise.

clue.text: Agree when despatched, from the sound of it

indicators.note: says the two short words, spoken together, run into a single word

parts.note: as can mean while or at the time that
despatched means sent off

explanation.surface: Someone agrees to something once it has been posted off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from the sound of it' says the phrase 'as sent', spoken, is the answer; here the spelling is identical, so the two words simply run together.
explanation.definitionFit: To give consent is to say yes to a proposal.

clue.text: Old Gaelic lake-dwelling that makes Ann go back after credit

indicators.note: after places the name and the turned word behind the credit abbreviation

parts.note: CR is the standard abbreviation for credit in accounts
the name taken as written

indicators.note: back tells us the word go is read from right to left

parts.note: taken as written before being turned round

explanation.surface: An archaeology note about an ancient Irish lake-house that forces Ann to retreat after some praise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the little word round; 'after' places Ann and that word behind the credit abbreviation. 'makes' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A prehistoric fortified island dwelling built in a lake in Ireland or Scotland.

clue.text: Payments torn from a student at Stourhead

parts.note: rent is the past participle of rend, to tear
L is the learner driver's plate, a student
the head of the word Stour is its first letter, S

explanation.surface: Charges levied on a student visiting Stourhead, the National Trust garden in Wiltshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Stourhead is a famous landscape garden in Wiltshire; split it as 'Stour head', the head of Stour.
explanation.definitionFit: Sums paid regularly for the hire of a property or equipment.

clue.text: Unwatered stock…

definitions.meaning: a spirit served without water or mixer

explanation.definitionFit: Spirits taken undiluted are served straight, and an archaic word for oxen or cattle is the same five-letter-less word.

clue.text: … freely distributed to investors

parts.note: continues the previous clue: shares handed out free to existing shareholders in a company

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue, stock given out for nothing to those who invest.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links to the clue before: 'stock... freely distributed to investors' describes a bonus share allotment.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonus allotment of new shares given without charge to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings.

clue.text: Pompously solemn canvas shelter with permeable coverage

indicators.note: coverage means one word wraps around the other, so the shelter sits within the permeable word

parts.note: porous means letting fluid pass through
a tent is a shelter made of canvas

explanation.surface: Describes a leaky tent while pretending to describe a pompous manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with permeable coverage' says the porous word covers TENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Overly grave and self-important, as in a weighty pronouncement.

clue.text: Boy about to pocket a ball with unerring accuracy

indicators.note: about means the boy word goes around the other piece

parts.note: a son is a boy
in snooker, to pot is to sink a ball into a pocket

explanation.surface: A lad gets ready to sink a snooker ball with perfect aim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the boy round the snooker verb. 'Pocket' looks like a noun here, but it is part of the verb phrase for sinking a ball.
explanation.definitionFit: Exactly right or precise, British informal for perfectly accurate.

clue.text: What footballers should be when they are thinking of marriage

definitions.text: What footballers should be when they are thinking of marriage

parts.words: What footballers should be when they are thinking of marriage
parts.note: a match is a marriage and fit means suitable, while footballers want to be in condition for a game

explanation.surface: A question about the state players should be in when they consider getting married.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'match' is both a game and a marriage; footballers need to be ready for one.
explanation.definitionFit: In good enough physical condition to play a game.

clue.text: An outspoken llanero?

parts.note: a llanero is a cowboy of the South American plains; outspoken suggests plain-speaking, so the phrase can mean both a frank person and a dweller on the plains

explanation.surface: A frank South American cowboy.
explanation.walkthrough: The llanos are the grassy plains of Venezuela and Colombia, whose herdsmen are llaneros; an outspoken person is plain-spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordinary, straightforward person who speaks frankly, also a dweller on the plains.

clue.text: Fight to include a Sussex abbey in a tourist itinerary?

definitions.text: to include a Sussex abbey in a tourist itinerary?
definitions.meaning: tourists 'do' a place when visiting it, and Battle is an East Sussex town with an abbey on the site of the battle of Hastings

explanation.definitionFit: To take up arms against an enemy, and to visit the East Sussex town with its abbey as a sightseer.

clue.text: Primitive canoe discovered by an archaeological expedition?

definitions.meaning: a boat made by hollowing out a tree trunk

explanation.definitionFit: A simple boat hollowed from a log, and an object found by excavation.

clue.text: Inexperienced young reporters describing an island folk in the Caribbean

indicators.note: describing is used in its sense of drawing around, so the reporters enclose the next word

parts.note: cub reporters are trainee journalists

explanation.surface: Novice journalists writing about a Caribbean island's people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describing' is used in its geometric sense of drawing a line round something, so the trainee reporters enclose 'an'.
explanation.definitionFit: People from the largest Caribbean island, whose capital is Havana.

clue.text: Military leader getting out a swell whip for punishment

indicators.note: getting, as the swell receives the officer, puts the leader within the wave word

parts.note: a surge is a swell of the sea
CO is the abbreviation for commanding officer

explanation.surface: An army commander rides a wave while wielding a lash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting' works as 'taking in': the swell takes in the commanding officer. 'Swell' looks like an adjective (fine), but it is the noun for a heave of the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A lash used to flog wrongdoers, as in a flagellant's instrument.

clue.text: Bleach when it goes in

indicators.note: goes in tells us the next word is placed within the first

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions on when to add bleach to the wash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes in' means the word it is placed inside the word when. The surface reads like laundry instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: To make something paler or colourless, as bleach does.

clue.text: Fresh clue to go on?

definitions.note: the noun is a signal to go on, so the definition is a description of its use

parts.note: green means fresh or new
a light is something that gives enlightenment, a clue

explanation.surface: Asking whether a new hint is enough to proceed.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: a traffic signal that tells drivers to go on, hence permission to proceed.
explanation.definitionFit: Permission to proceed, from the traffic signal that tells drivers to move.

clue.text: I go round after a discount on foreign bills

indicators.note: after places the rearranged letters behind the article
round says the letters of I go are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: A banker's note about a reduction on foreign bills of exchange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' rearranges I GO into GIO, and 'after' sets it behind A.
explanation.definitionFit: The percentage charged when exchanging one currency or bill for another.

clue.text: What we put on the plate when in church?

definitions.text: What we put on the plate when in church?

parts.words: What we put on the plate when in church?
parts.note: the collection plate passed round in church receives money, not food

explanation.surface: A question about a church collection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plate' suggests food; it is the collection plate passed round during a service.
explanation.definitionFit: Money in notes and coins, given at the offertory.

clue.text: Distinctive garb that never varies

definitions.meaning: clothing worn by members of a group such as soldiers or schoolchildren

explanation.definitionFit: Standard dress worn by a group, and something constant and unchanging throughout.

clue.text: A tower of strength on the farm, maybe

definitions.text: A tower of strength on the farm, maybe

parts.words: A tower of strength on the farm, maybe
parts.note: a tower here is something that tows, and the strength is engine power on a farm

explanation.surface: Praise for a dependable farmhand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tower of strength' is a reliable person; read 'tower' as one that tows: a powerful farm vehicle pulling ploughs and trailers.
explanation.definitionFit: A powerful farm vehicle used for pulling ploughs and trailers.

clue.text: Official responsible for man who has been arrested?

definitions.meaning: someone with authority over a task
a person held on a criminal charge

explanation.definitionFit: The one in authority, and someone held by police on a criminal accusation.
